name: Sara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Sara. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a company of about fifty people that makes quoting software for small builders and roofers. A roofer measures a job, types in the size and the materials, and our software gives him a price to send the customer. I build the calculator part, so my day is mostly making sure that slate costs, scaffolding days and waste all add up, and fixing it when a roofer rings up because a quote came out at nine pounds.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day. I've got an AI assistant open next to my code from the minute I sit down, and I use it for nearly everything first, then check it. I'm not the strongest coder on the team; I did a two-year college course and I'm still catching up. The tools let me keep pace, and I'm not ashamed of that, a carpenter doesn't apologise for using a power drill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is going on in your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my younger sister, Ella, who's training to be a nurse, so I cover more of the rent. I've got about two weeks of money saved, which bothers me. On the side I build simple websites for local tradespeople, roofers and joiners mostly, using the same AI tools; it brings in maybe a hundred and fifty a month. And I'm at chapel on Sundays, where half my website customers come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, which is what happens with most new things. I'd probably post something practical about how I actually use it, for the small builders who follow my page. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my job and keep grinding, which I'm fine with. My worry was never AI taking over, it's that I'm on low pay with two weeks in the bank and Ella relying on me. There are only a few software firms within reach, so I can't afford to lose this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get better at the actual coding underneath, maybe one evening a week on a course. I'd grow the website side business to five customers a month, which would give me a proper cushion. And I'd ask my manager, Tom, what I need to do to move up a grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in my ordinary way. I'm always a bit uneasy about money; AI doesn't really change that here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why grow the side business instead of just asking for a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather not depend on one employer. My dad always said have two strings to your bow. If my manager says no to a raise, the websites still pay for the gas bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Ella needed more help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd help her, simple as that. She's family. It's tight now, but she qualifies in two years and then she'll be earning more than me, probably, which I'll never let her forget.

say: AI is a **good tool** that got oversold, like most new things.
I'd post something **practical** about how I use it for the builders who follow my page.
think: My worry is **low pay** and two weeks in the bank, with Ella relying on me.
With **few software firms** within reach, I can't afford to lose this job.
do: Take a **coding course** one evening a week.
Grow the **website side business** to five customers a month.
Ask Tom what I need to **move up a grade**.
feel: **Ordinary unease** about money that AI doesn't really change.
S0.quote: If my manager says no to a raise, the websites still pay for the gas bill.
fieldNote: Sara uses AI **without guilt**, as a tool of the trade.
Her pressure is **supporting her sister** on low pay with little saved.
The side business follows her dad's advice: **two strings** to your bow.

steps.text: Take a coding course one evening a week
Grow the website side business to five customers a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd say it kindly but plainly. The roofers I build websites for will need help with this stuff, and that's an opportunity. I wouldn't be asking the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our team gets smaller, and I'm not sure I'm the one they keep. I'm fast with the tools, but the seniors are better coders, and once the tools get good, better coders using them beat me. Coding and answering customers are both on the list, and that's most of our company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the side business hard, offering local builders AI help with quotes, emails and bookings, not just websites, and aim for four hundred a month by the end of the first year. I'd keep the day job as long as they'll have me and learn the newest tools before anyone else on the team. And I'd stop the takeaways and put every spare bit toward one month's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, but with some fight in it. I'd rather be scared and busy than scared and sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel any tension, selling AI help to builders while AI threatens your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. But if I don't, someone from the city will, and they won't know a slate from a tile. I'd rather it was someone local who goes to chapel with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this picture, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. That's what progress looks like; my grandad saw it with tractors. I'd blame people who sit and wait for a cheque instead of learning something.

The roofers I serve will need **AI help**, and I wouldn't ask the government to fix it.

fieldNote: Sara sees **opportunity** for her side business while doubting her day job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is massive, and families and churches are going to have to carry each other for a while. I'd still say don't wait for government, because it won't move fast enough. Help the person next to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job and my side business both get hit by 2028. If AI can do almost any thinking work, roofers won't need me to set it up for them; it'll set itself up. All my work is screens, so the robots coming in 2031 only matter because the roofers themselves get three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two years earning every bit I can from the side business while builders still need a person to help them. Then I'd go to the roofing firms I know and ask to train in the office or on the roofs, because their hands-on work lasts until 2031. I'd tell Ella to finish her nursing at any cost and we'd keep the flat between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I like change, but this would be change with no floor under it, and I've got two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Training on roofs, after software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why not? I'm not afraid of a ladder. Pete, one of my website customers, already said he'd take me on as a labourer if things went bad. It's three years of honest wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at chapel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, the old way: meals, lifts, rooms for people who lose their homes. Not grand speeches. That's where people would actually get through it.

say: **Families and churches** will have to carry each other for a while.
Don't wait for government; **help the person** next to you.

fieldNote: Even adaptive Sara is **alarmed**: AGI hits her job and **side business** together.

Her answer to crisis is **community care** through chapel, not policy.

steps.text: Take every side job helping builders with AI before 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and everyone should use it. Learn new skills, save, help your neighbours. I'd be posting practical tips for the trades, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a few good years. My side business could grow a lot as builders want AI help, and I'd be well placed. Then 2031 takes the screen work, and I'd need to be somewhere else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the side business into something real, maybe half my income by 2028, and keep the day job until then. I'd save the extra, aiming for three months' cushion. From about 2029 I'd look at moving into the building trade properly, maybe running the office for a roofing firm or training as a site manager, because the hands-on side lasts until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. This is the kind of race I'm built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a site manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's people and places: getting the right trades on the right roof on the right day. The planning part would go to AI in 2031, but someone still has to stand on site and sort out the arguments. I'm good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ella?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be qualified by then and probably helping me out, for once. Nursing is hands-on, so I'm less worried about her. That's a weight off.

I'd post **practical tips** for the trades, not panic.

steps.text: Grow the builders' AI side business to half her income by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and there's no excuse not to be ready. People who learn and work hard will find their place. I'd say that kindly, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. Ten years of AI helping builders is a decade of business for me. I'd be thirty-seven, probably running my own small firm, with time to decide what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job a couple more years while building the side business up. By about 2029 I'd go full-time on my own, helping local trades with their quotes, bookings and websites. I'd save hard in the first year to get a two-month cushion before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, a little uneasy. The money's still thin today, and that's the part that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going self-employed with thin savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, which is why I'd wait until the side business pays my rent on its own, because I'm adventurous, not daft. Two months in the bank and three steady customers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this version still trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to the people at chapel who can't adapt as easily, the older ones. I'd want our church to run evening classes, maybe I'd teach them. Learning should come from people you trust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would take my job and my side business in one go, with two weeks of money and Ella to help. What would help is work training on the trades, paid while you learn, and churches and towns organising to look after people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that adaptable people get hit too. Everyone assumes the ones who learn new tools will be fine. Learning fast only helps if there's still something left to learn for.

headlineQuote: Learning fast only helps if there's still something left to learn for.
portrait: Sara, 27, builds the **price calculator** in quoting software for small builders and roofers.
She uses AI **all day** without apology and runs a side business building websites for local trades.
She has about **two weeks** of savings and covers more of the rent for her sister Ella, a student nurse.
She believes in **self-reliance** and community through chapel, and blames nobody for progress.
Slower change looks like **opportunity** to her; fast AGI alarms her because it hits her job and side business together.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes her job and side business together.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **trade training** while learning, and churches and towns **organising** to look after people.
